title: Journey Maps
strapline: Big paper, fat pens and the route from your front door to here — the first map you ever draw.
intent: Children develop an understanding of journeys, places and the order things come in.
Drawing a route is purposeful mark-making with real meaning behind it.
Sequencing landmarks — first the postbox, then the shop, then nursery — is early narrative structure.
Children's own local knowledge becomes the content, so every child has something to say.
Talking through a route while drawing it builds sustained, connected talk.
implementation: Provide large paper and pens so children can draw a simple map — home to nursery, to the park, on holiday.
Add stickers for roads, trees and houses so a child who cannot yet draw them is not stuck.
Model drawing a road or path first, thinking aloud about what you pass on the way.
Ask questions that prompt sequence: what do we see first, and then what?
Scribe children's commentary onto the map in their own words.
Encourage storytelling over accuracy — the journey matters more than the geography.
Display the maps together and let children walk each other through them.
key_questions: What do we see on the way to nursery?
What comes first on your journey, and what comes next?
How do you travel — do you walk, drive, take the bus?
Where would you like your map to go to?
Can you show me on your map where you live?

impact.text: Children draw with intent and can tell you what their marks mean.
Children make marks with communicated meaning — labels, signs, routes.
Children recount a real journey in rough sequence.
Children use positional language in their talk — next to, behind, past, along.
Children know their local patch and the people and places in it.
Children hold a back-and-forth conversation about something they know well.

enhancements: A giant floor map of the local area built from a printed aerial photo.
A walk along a real short route, then map it together on return.
A small world town laid over the maps so cars can drive the drawn routes.
A treasure map version with a hidden X somewhere in the nursery garden.
A photo trail of local landmarks for children to place on a shared map.
A map-reading challenge — follow a friend's map and see where you end up.

playing_exploring: Children choose their own journey and draw it however they see it.
Stickers and pens invite open, unpressured mark-making.
active_learning: Children work at a large map for a sustained stretch, adding detail.
They come back to add more as they remember it.
creating_thinking: Children order a route in sequence and reason about what comes next.
They represent a real three-dimensional world on flat paper, which is a real leap.
